clinicalPearls: PSVT here refers to sustained supraventricular tachycardias that depend on the AV node: AVNRT, junctional tachycardia, AV reciprocating tachycardia (AVRT) using an accessory pathway, and preexcited tachycardias (Harrison 22e p.1938).

AVNRT is the most common form of PSVT, accounting for roughly 60% of cases referred for catheter ablation, typically presenting in the second to fourth decades and more often in women (Harrison 22e p.1939).

AVNRT mechanism is reentry within the AV node and perinodal atrium, made possible by dual conduction pathways; the typical form uses a slowly conducting pathway (right inferior nodal extension) for the antegrade limb and the fast pathway as the exit (Harrison 22e p.1939).

In typical AVNRT atrial and ventricular activation are near-simultaneous, so the P wave falls during, just before, or just after the QRS and is hard to see — often appearing as a pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S waves in leads II, III, and aVF (Harrison 22e p.1939).

Simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction drives atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve, producing cannon A waves and a fluttering neck sensation; elevated venous pressure can release natriuretic peptides causing post-tachycardia diuresis (Harrison 22e p.1939).
Unlike atrial tachycardias, maneuvers or drugs that block the AV node terminate AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT, because the AV node is part of the reentry circuit (Harrison 22e p.1939).

Accessory pathways occur in about 1 in 1500-2000 people; most patients have structurally normal hearts, but APs are associated with Ebstein's anomaly and certain hypertrophic cardiomyopathies including PRKAG2 mutations, Danon's disease, and Fabry's disease (Harrison 22e p.1940).
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is defined as ventricular preexcitation during sinus rhythm (short PR <0.12 s, delta wave, widened QRS) plus episodes of PSVT (Harrison 22e p.1940).

Orthodromic AVRT is the most common AP-mediated PSVT: the wavefront goes antegrade down the AV node/His-Purkinje and returns retrograde up the AP, giving a narrow (or aberrant) QRS with the P wave always following the QRS, never simultaneous with it (Harrison 22e p.1941).
Concealed accessory pathways conduct only retrograde (ventricle to atrium), so no preexcitation is seen in sinus rhythm, yet SVT can still occur (Harrison 22e pp.1940-1941).

Antidromic AVRT and bystander AP conduction produce preexcited (wide-complex) tachycardias that can be indistinguishable from monomorphic VT; the presence of preexcitation in sinus rhythm suggests the diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.1941-1942).

Junctional ectopic tachycardia arises from automaticity within the AV node, is rare in adults, and is more often seen as an incessant tachycardia in children, especially perioperatively after congenital heart surgery (Harrison 22e p.1940).
harrison.pathophysiology: PSVTs in this group are AV node-dependent. AVNRT is a reentrant circuit within the compact AV node and perinodal atrium enabled by dual pathways: a slowly conducting pathway (usually the right inferior nodal extension running toward the coronary sinus floor) and a faster pathway near the His bundle, allowing a self-sustaining loop. Accessory pathways are congenital muscular connections that bridge atrium and ventricle across the fibrous AV rings owing to incomplete partitioning during development; they most often lie at the left free wall, followed by posteroseptal, right free wall, and anteroseptal sites. Antegrade conduction over an AP produces ventricular preexcitation (short PR, delta wave, wide QRS), with QRS/delta morphology determined by pathway location. AVRT reentry circulates between the AV node/His-Purkinje system and the AP (orthodromic when antegrade over the node and retrograde over the AP, antidromic when reversed). Junctional ectopic tachycardia is due to abnormal automaticity within the AV node rather than reentry (Harrison 22e pp.1938-1942).
additionalDifferentials: Orthodromic AV reciprocating tachycardia (concealed or manifest AP)
Atypical AVNRT (long R-P, P wave between QRS complexes)
Permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT) from a slowly conducting septal AP
nonInfectiousMimics: Ventricular tachycardia (especially versus antidromic AVRT or PSVT with aberrancy, wide-complex tachycardia)
Lateral or inferior wall myocardial infarction Q waves (mimicked by negative delta waves of left-sided or diaphragmatic accessory pathways)
Bundle branch block pattern (mimicked by preexcitation: right-sided AP gives LBBB-like V1, left-sided AP gives RBBB-like V1)
additionalInvestigations: Continuous ECG monitoring during the episode and during vagal/pharmacologic maneuvers (the response can establish the mechanism)
12-lead ECG during tachycardia (P-wave timing and morphology, pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in inferior leads) and during sinus rhythm (delta wave, short PR)
Echocardiography to exclude Ebstein's anomaly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy associated with APs, or tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
Invasive electrophysiology study to define mechanism and to assess whether an AP can support rapid antegrade conduction (risk stratification)
Ambulatory monitoring or exercise testing to look for abrupt loss of preexcitation suggesting a lower-risk pathway (not completely reliable)
redFlags: Hemodynamic instability with hypotension, loss of consciousness, or respiratory distress
Preexcited atrial fibrillation presenting as a very irregular wide-complex tachycardia
Accessory pathway with shortest preexcited R-R interval <250 ms during AF (about 25% of preexcitation-causing APs), associated with higher risk of ventricular fibrillation and sudden death
Wide-complex tachycardia that cannot be confidently distinguished from VT (manage as VT until proven otherwise)
Rapid SVT in the elderly precipitating angina, pulmonary edema, hypotension, or syncope
harrison.prognosis: In patients without structural heart disease, AVNRT is not life-threatening though it may cause significant symptoms. Catheter ablation of the slow AV nodal pathway is curative in over 95% of cases, with a risk of AV block requiring permanent pacing in under 1%. For accessory pathways, ablation efficacy is around 95% (varies by location) with serious complications in under 3% and procedural mortality under 1 in 1000. Risk of cardiac arrest in symptomatic preexcitation patients is roughly 2 per 1000 adults and likely higher in children. Adults with asymptomatic preexcitation have an estimated sudden death risk of about 1 per 1000 patient-years, while children carry a higher risk of around 2 per 1000 patient-years (Harrison 22e pp.1939-1942).
pitfalls: Administering AV nodal-blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem, beta blockers, adenosine, amiodarone) during preexcited AF is contraindicated, as slowing the AV node without slowing the AP can accelerate ventricular rate and precipitate ventricular fibrillation (Harrison 22e p.1942).

Gradual loss of AP conduction with rising sympathetic tone on exercise testing does not reliably indicate a low-risk pathway, because it can simply reflect shortening AV nodal conduction time (Harrison 22e p.1942).
Adenosine itself can precipitate atrial fibrillation in up to ~15% of patients, which is hazardous in WPW where AF may cause hemodynamic instability (Harrison 22e p.1942).
Adenosine is contraindicated after cardiac transplantation due to denervation hypersensitivity and may aggravate bronchospasm (Harrison 22e p.1942).
Negative delta waves from left-sided or diaphragmatic/paraseptal APs can mimic Q waves of lateral or inferior myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.1940).
Left free wall APs may show minimal or absent preexcitation on the 12-lead ECG because of the distance from the sinus node, so preexcitation can be missed (Harrison 22e p.1940).
PJRT and atypical AVNRT both produce long R-P tachycardias that can be difficult to distinguish from atrial tachycardia without an invasive EP study (Harrison 22e p.1941).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity grading scale; risk is stratified clinically by hemodynamic stability and, for accessory pathways, by the capacity for rapid antegrade conduction. A shortest preexcited R-R interval <250 ms during atrial fibrillation marks a high-risk pathway predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (Harrison 22e p.1942).
management: Terminate acute AV-node-dependent episodes with vagal manoeuvres such as a modified Valsalva, escalating to intravenous adenosine
Perform synchronised DC cardioversion for haemodynamically unstable tachycardia
Use intravenous AV-nodal-blocking agents such as verapamil, diltiazem, or a beta-blocker when adenosine fails
Offer catheter ablation of the slow AV-nodal pathway or accessory pathway as curative, first-line definitive therapy for recurrent symptomatic disease
Provide chronic suppression with beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers for patients who decline or defer ablation
In ventricular pre-excitation, avoid AV-nodal-blocking drugs during pre-excited atrial fibrillation and refer for electrophysiological risk stratification and ablation
Teach patients self-administered vagal manoeuvres and refer to a cardiac electrophysiology service
